unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Coppermill Furniture Ltd is a private limited company in Redbrook, Country X, manufacturing oak dining tables and chairs. It employs 34 workers and recorded sales revenue of $2.6 million last year. In 2023 it borrowed $400,000 from its bank at 5% annual interest to buy machinery. Two years of repayments have been made and the outstanding balance is $300,000.

The central bank has raised its base rate from 5% to 9%, so the rate on the outstanding balance will rise to 9% next month, adding $12,000 a year to interest costs. Owner Priya Raman wants to open a second workshop costing $180,000, funded by a further loan at 10% costing about $18,000 a year in interest. The order book is full for the next 6 months, but Priya fears customers may spend less if rates stay high. She must decide whether to expand now or wait until rates fall.

questions.question_text: Identify two effects of a rise in interest rates on a business with a bank loan.
questions.model_answer: One effect is higher interest payments on the outstanding loan, which reduce profit. A second effect is less cash available to fund other spending or expansion, which may force the business to delay plans. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest payments on an existing loan reduce profit
Higher borrowing costs make new loans more expensive

questions.question_text: Explain two effects of the interest rate rise on Coppermill Furniture Ltd.
questions.model_answer: Higher interest costs: the rise from 5% to 9% on the $300,000 outstanding balance adds $12,000 a year, which will reduce Coppermill's profit [k], and this extra cost arrives while the machinery loan taken out in 2023 is still being repaid [app]. More expensive expansion finance: the proposed second workshop would need a further loan at 10%, costing about $18,000 a year in interest [k], which may make the $180,000 expansion hard to justify if customers spend less while rates stay high [app].

knowledge_max_2: Interest payments on an existing loan increase when rates rise
New borrowing becomes more expensive when rates rise
application_max_2: The outstanding balance is $300,000, so the rise from 5% to 9% adds $12,000 a year
The proposed $180,000 workshop loan at 10% would cost about $18,000 a year in interest

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why rising interest rates might reduce demand for Coppermill's furniture.
questions.model_answer: Higher mortgage and loan payments: rising interest rates increase the cost of borrowing for households [k], so buyers of oak dining furniture already stretched by higher monthly repayments have less money to spend [app]. As buyers postpone big-ticket purchases, Coppermill's order book may shorten from its current 6 months, cutting future revenue [an]. Attractive savings returns: higher rates make saving more rewarding, so households save rather than spend [k], meaning demand for non-essential items like oak furniture falls [app], which would leave Coppermill with unsold stock and lower cash inflow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for consumers
Higher interest rates make saving more attractive than spending
application_max_2: Coppermill makes big-ticket items such as oak dining tables, which are often financed by borrowing
Coppermill fears customers may spend less if rates stay high
analysis_max_2: Higher mortgage and loan repayments reduce disposable income and big-ticket demand
More saving means less spending on non-essential furniture, cutting future sales

questions.question_text: Do you think Priya Raman should proceed with the $180,000 expansion now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Proceeding now would let Coppermill open the second workshop while its order book is full for the next 6 months [k], spreading the $18,000 a year interest on a $180,000 loan across higher sales [app], so profit could rise and the firm could win customers from rivals [an]. However, the rise from 5% to 9% already adds $12,000 a year to existing loan costs, and customers may spend less so demand could drop below the order book's promise [k], leaving the new loan hard to repay on only $2.6 million of sales [app], and serving two loans at once could push the business into debt it cannot service [an]. On balance, Priya should proceed but with caution, for example by confirming orders before signing the loan [eval], because the order book is full and waiting could mean missing the selling season when rates fall [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Expansion can increase output and sales while demand is strong
Higher interest rates increase repayment burdens and financial risk
application_max_2: The order book is full for the next 6 months at time the 9% rate takes effect
Existing loan balance of $300,000 now costs $12,000 a year extra; expansion loan would cost $18,000 a year
analysis_max_2: New capacity could lift output and win market share before demand falls
If sales fall, the business may be unable to service the additional loan
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation (proceed with caution or confirm orders first)
Judgement weighs short-term opportunity against borrowing risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Halden Motors is an independent car dealership in Dunmore, Country X, selling new and used family cars. It employs 12 sales staff and 6 service technicians, and sold 210 cars last year with revenue of $4.3 million. Around 70% of buyers use finance packages arranged through the dealership, and the average new car costs about $19,000.

The central bank has cut its base interest rate from 6% to 3% to encourage spending. Weekly finance applications at Halden Motors have risen from 18 to 29, and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts. Owner Mr Whitmore must decide whether to borrow $250,000 to buy in 40 additional new cars before the peak sales season, or keep his current stock of 90 cars and rely more on used vehicles.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by the 'base rate' of interest.
questions.model_answer: The base rate is the interest rate set by a country's central bank. It influences the rates commercial banks charge on loans and pay on savings, so a cut makes borrowing cheaper. [2]

knowledge_max_2: The base rate is set by the central bank
The base rate influences commercial bank lending and saving rates

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why the interest rate cut may increase Halden Motors' car sales.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper borrowing for buyers: cutting the base rate from 6% to 3% reduces monthly finance payments on cars [k], and with 70% of Halden's buyers using finance packages, more customers can afford a new $19,000 car [app]. Borrowing is now more attractive than saving: lower rates make saving less rewarding and credit cheaper [k], which is why weekly finance applications have jumped from 18 to 29 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing
Lower interest rates reduce the reward for saving
application_max_2: Around 70% of Halden's buyers use finance packages and the average new car costs about $19,000
Weekly finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 since the cut from 6% to 3%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Halden Motors of borrowing $250,000 to buy 40 additional new cars.
questions.model_answer: Meeting rising demand: sales applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week and rival dealers are expanding their forecourts [k], so having 40 extra cars ready before the peak sales season would let Halden capture sales rather than lose buyers to competitors [app]. More cars in stock lifts potential revenue by roughly 40 x $19,000 = $760,000 [an]. Economies of bulk buying: ordering 40 cars at once may earn volume discounts from manufacturers [k], reducing the cost of each additional car [app], and with finance demand this strong the extra stock should sell quickly, protecting cash flow [an].

knowledge_max_2: Having more stock lets a business meet demand and avoid lost sales
Buying in bulk can reduce the cost per unit
application_max_2: Finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week and rivals are expanding forecourts
The peak sales season is approaching and new cars average about $19,000
analysis_max_2: Extra stock captures demand that would otherwise go to rivals
Higher sales volume raises revenue and cash inflow

questions.question_text: Do you think Mr Whitmore should borrow $250,000 to buy 40 additional new cars? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Buying the cars would let Halden Motors exploit the surge in finance applications, from 18 to 29 a week, while rival dealers are already expanding [k], so acting now could capture sales worth roughly 40 x $19,000 = $760,000 [app], lifting profit and market share in Dunmore [an]. However, borrowing $250,000 adds interest costs and risk if the slowdown deepens [k]; used vehicles already cost nothing extra to finance and may be all that cautious customers need [app], and if rates rise again before the stock sells, margins could be squeezed [an]. On balance, Mr Whitmore should borrow to buy the cars, but order them in stages matched to confirmed orders [eval], because the evidence of demand (29 applications a week, up from 18) points to strong sales [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Buying more stock lets a business exploit rising demand
Borrowing increases costs and financial risk if sales disappoint
application_max_2: Finance applications have risen from 18 to 29 a week after the cut from 6% to 3%
The average new car costs about $19,000 and 70% of buyers use finance
analysis_max_2: Extra stock could secure substantial additional revenue and market share
If demand weakens, unsold cars create a heavy interest and storage burden
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation with a clear position on the $250,000 loan
Judgement weighs demand evidence against borrowing risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Thistledown Home & Living is a private limited company operating 4 homewares stores across Country X, employing 58 staff and recording revenue of $3.4 million last year. It sells bedding, kitchenware and furniture to middle-income households. Since the central bank raised the base interest rate from 4% to 7%, customer visits have fallen by 18% and like-for-like sales dropped 12% in the first quarter. Savings accounts now pay 6% interest.

Owner Carla Ng must decide how to respond. One option is to cut prices by 15% on bedding and kitchenware to attract price-sensitive shoppers; at current volumes she estimates the margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents. The other option is to reduce next season's stock orders by 25% and cut staff hours by 10% to protect cash flow. Store rents cost $9,000 per store per month regardless of sales.

questions.question_text: State what is meant by 'consumer spending'.
questions.model_answer: Consumer spending is the total amount of money households spend on goods and services. When consumers spend more, business sales and demand tend to rise. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Consumer spending is household expenditure on goods and services
Higher consumer spending increases demand for business products

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Thistledown's sales have fallen since interest rates rose.
questions.model_answer: Borrowing is now more expensive: the rise from 4% to 7% increases mortgage, loan and credit costs for households [k], so customers on middle incomes have less money to spend on homewares [app]. Saving is now more attractive: with savings accounts paying 6% interest, households prefer to save rather than spend [k], which is why store visits have fallen 18% and like-for-like sales have dropped 12% in the first quarter [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive
Higher interest rates make saving more attractive
application_max_2: Thistledown sells to middle-income households across 4 stores generating $3.4 million last year
Customer visits have fallen 18% and like-for-like sales dropped 12% in the first quarter

questions.question_text: Explain two problems for Thistledown of cutting prices by 15%.
questions.model_answer: Lower profit per sale: a 15% price cut reduces the margin on each $1 of sales from 38 cents to around 27 cents [k], while rents of $9,000 per store per month still have to be paid [app], so sales volumes must rise just to stand still and profit could disappear [an]. Possible price war: competitors may match the cut, removing the sales gain [k], leaving Thistledown with thinner margins and no increase in volume [app], which could push the business towards cash-flow difficulties [an].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices reduces the profit earned per unit
Competitors may match a price cut, limiting any sales gain
application_max_2: The margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents
Store rents cost $9,000 per store per month regardless of sales across 4 stores
analysis_max_2: Revenue must rise just to cover unchanged costs, squeezing profit
A price war could leave the business worse off with no volume gain

questions.question_text: Do you think Carla Ng should cut prices by 15% on bedding and kitchenware? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting prices could attract price-sensitive shoppers back into the 4 stores [k], and keeping some visitors spending beats empty stores paying $9,000 rent [app], which might rebuild visitor numbers and protect sales volumes [an]. However, the cut would reduce profit on existing sales while rents of $9,000 per store per month remain fixed [k], and if competitors match it, Thistledown gains nothing [app], pushing the business towards cash-flow problems while still needing to protect 58 jobs [an]. On balance, Carla should not cut prices across the board; she should use modest promotions together with the stock and staffing reductions [eval], because the margin fall from 38 cents to 27 cents makes a 15% cut too deep to sustain [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Lower prices can stimulate demand and attract price-sensitive customers
Cutting prices reduces profit margins and may not increase revenue if demand is weak
application_max_2: Margin on each $1 of sales would fall from 38 cents to around 27 cents on a 15% cut
Rents of $9,000 per store per month over 4 stores are fixed, and sales fell 12% in the first quarter
analysis_max_2: A cut could rebuild traffic and protect sales volumes
If rivals match the cut, profit falls with no volume gain, worsening cash flow
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on whether to cut prices
Judgement weighs a margin of 38 to 27 cents against the need to keep customers

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Saltwood Coffee Roasters is a private limited company in Country X, supplying roasted coffee beans to 240 independent cafés. It employs 16 staff and produced 320,000 bags of 1kg coffee last year with revenue of $2.9 million. Over the last 12 months, inflation in Country X has reached 9.5%. Green coffee bean costs are up 40%, roasting energy up 22%, and wages for packing staff up 8%.

Saltwood sells a 1kg wholesale bag for $24.00, but its production cost has risen from $17.50 to $21.00 per bag. Managing director Tomás Ibero must decide whether to raise the wholesale price to $27.50 next month, a 14.6% increase, or hold prices and accept a lower profit margin to keep loyal café customers. Two key café customers have already complained about the smaller price rises Saltwood made in 2025.

questions.question_text: Outline two ways high inflation can affect a business.
questions.model_answer: One way is that input costs such as raw materials, energy and wages rise, squeezing profit margins. A second way is that consumers' purchasing power falls, so demand may drop as customers spend less. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises the cost of inputs such as materials, energy and wages
Inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power, lowering demand

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Saltwood's profit margin has fallen.
questions.model_answer: Rising input costs: inflation of 9.5% has pushed green coffee bean costs up 40% and roastery energy up 22% [k], so the cost of producing a 1kg bag has climbed from $17.50 to $21.00 [app]. Wage increases: packing staff wages have risen 8% [k], adding to costs that cannot be passed on while the wholesale price is held at $24.00 [app].

knowledge_max_2: Rising input costs reduce profit margins
Rising wage costs increase production expenses
application_max_2: Green coffee bean costs are up 40% and roasting energy up 22%
Production cost per bag has risen from $17.50 to $21.00 with wages up 8%

questions.question_text: Explain two risks for Saltwood of raising the wholesale price to $27.50.
questions.model_answer: Loss of café customers: raising prices by 14.6% may push price-sensitive cafés to cheaper suppliers [k], while two key café customers already complained about Saltwood's smaller 2025 price rises [app], so losing their weekly orders would cut volume across the 240 café network [an]. Reduced demand: higher wholesale prices may force cafés to raise their own prices, reducing café footfall [k], which passes inflation pressure onto end customers [app], shrinking Saltwood's sales and making the recovery of its 12.5% margin harder [an].

knowledge_max_2: Higher prices may push customers to cheaper suppliers
Higher prices can reduce demand
application_max_2: Two key café customers already complained about smaller price rises in 2025
Saltwood supplies 240 independent cafés and a 14.6% rise is proposed
analysis_max_2: Losing café customers cuts sales volume and revenue
Passing costs on to cafés may reduce end-consumer demand

questions.question_text: Do you think Saltwood should raise the wholesale price from $24.00 to $27.50? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Raising the price would restore Saltwood's margin: at $27.50 against a $21.00 cost, margin would rise from 12.5% to about 24% [k], and with bean costs up 40%, holding $24.00 would destroy profit on 320,000 bags a year [app], threatening the jobs of 16 staff [an]. However, a 14.6% increase may drive loyal café customers to rivals [k], and Saltwood has already faced complaints from two key customers in 2025 [app], so volume could fall and erase the benefit of the higher price [an]. On balance, Saltwood should raise the price, but by a smaller amount or with advance notice and quality assurances [eval], because the margin evidence shows it cannot absorb another year at 12.5% [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Raising price can restore profit margins when costs rise
Raising price risks losing customers to competitors
application_max_2: Production cost per bag rose from $17.50 to $21.00 while the price is held at $24.00
Two key café customers complained about the smaller 2025 price rises
analysis_max_2: A higher price protects profit and staff jobs
Volume loss from unhappy cafés could erase the margin gain
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the $27.50 price
Judgement weighs margin recovery against customer loyalty risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Eastmoor Budget Hotel is a private limited company in Millbrook, Country X, with 110 rooms near the Eastmoor industrial estate. It employs 42 staff and averages 55% occupancy, earning revenue of $2.4 million last year. In January the town's steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs, pushing local unemployment from 3.5% to 7.2%. Inflation rose to 8% in the same period and consumer confidence fell sharply.

General manager Denise Whitaker has noticed business bookings are down 30%, while enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers attending interviews have doubled. She must decide whether to cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65 to stimulate demand, or introduce weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests. The rate cut could fill 15 extra rooms a night, while weekly rates would give more predictable occupancy across the quiet summer months.

questions.question_text: Outline two effects of rising local unemployment on a business.
questions.model_answer: One effect is that consumers have less income to spend, so demand for products falls. A second effect is that more workers are available to hire, making recruitment easier and possibly cheaper. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces consumer incomes and demand
Higher unemployment increases the supply of labour available to businesses

questions.question_text: Explain two ways the factory closure has affected Eastmoor Budget Hotel.
questions.model_answer: Weaker demand from business travellers: the factory's closure with the loss of 900 jobs has cut local business activity and incomes [k], and Eastmoor has seen business bookings fall by 30% [app]. A new opportunity from long-stay guests: rising unemployment brings job-seekers needing affordable accommodation [k], shown by the doubling of enquiries for weekly rates [app].

knowledge_max_2: Higher unemployment reduces demand for business-related spending
Higher unemployment can increase demand for low-cost services from job-seekers
application_max_2: The steel components factory closed with the loss of 900 jobs and local unemployment rose from 3.5% to 7.2%
Business bookings are down 30% while enquiries for weekly rates have doubled

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Eastmoor of introducing weekly rates of $400 for long-stay guests.
questions.model_answer: More predictable occupancy: weekly rates give a guaranteed share of the 110 rooms each week [k], which suits the hotel's need for steady occupancy in the quiet summer months [app], improving cash flow and making staffing easier to plan [an]. Better use of empty rooms: at $400 a week the effective nightly rate is about $57, below the standard $80 rate but above a $65 cut applied to every room [k], so the hotel fills rooms that would otherwise stay empty [app], raising total revenue without discounting all rooms [an].

knowledge_max_2: Weekly rates provide predictable, guaranteed occupancy
Weekly rates can fill otherwise empty rooms without discounting all sales
application_max_2: Eastmoor averages 55% occupancy with 110 rooms to fill
Enquiries for weekly rates from job-seekers have doubled
analysis_max_2: Predictable occupancy improves cash flow and staffing plans
Filling rooms at an effective rate above the proposed cut protects revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Denise Whitaker should cut the nightly room rate from $80 to $65? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Cutting the nightly rate could attract price-conscious leisure guests [k], and filling 15 extra rooms a night at $65 would add about $975 of nightly revenue compared with empty rooms [app], lifting occupancy above 55% and spreading fixed costs over more guests [an]. However, the cut would reduce revenue on the rooms that would have been sold anyway [k], while weekly rates of $400 match the doubled demand from long-stay job-seekers without cutting standard prices [app], leaving the hotel worse off if existing guests simply switch from $80 to $65 [an]. On balance, the hotel should introduce the $400 weekly rate rather than cut the nightly price [eval], because it targets the proven demand, with enquiries doubled, at less risk to standard revenue [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Cutting prices can stimulate demand and fill spare capacity
Cutting prices reduces revenue on sales that would have happened anyway
application_max_2: The nightly rate would fall from $80 to $65 with a possible gain of 15 extra rooms a night
Weekly rates of $400 match doubled enquiries from job-seekers
analysis_max_2: 15 extra rooms a night adds around $975 nightly revenue and spreads fixed costs
Existing guests switching to the cheaper rate would cut revenue with no extra occupancy
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the nightly rate cut
Judgement weighs extra occupancy against reduced revenue on existing sales

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Drayton Packaging Co is a private limited company in Country X, manufacturing corrugated boxes for food exporters. It operates 2 factories, employs 130 workers and recorded revenue of $6.8 million last year. Country X's economy grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade, helped by consumer spending and food exports rising 14%. Drayton's order book has grown 25% in 9 months.

Sales director Owen Pryce projects orders will rise another 20% over the next 12 months. Drayton can either recruit 30 permanent workers at a total wage cost of $900,000 a year, or meet demand through overtime at time-and-a-half and subcontracted production, costing an extra $250,000 a year. Overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit, and two key customers want their supply contracts extended for 3 years.

questions.question_text: Define 'gross domestic product (GDP)'.
questions.model_answer: Gross domestic product (GDP) is the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a year. It is used to measure the size and growth of an economy. [2]

knowledge_max_2: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country
GDP is measured over a period, usually a year

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Drayton's sales have increased.
questions.model_answer: Economic growth: GDP grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade, so households and businesses spend more [k], lifting demand for packaged goods and therefore for corrugated boxes [app]. Strong exports: food exports have risen 14%, and Drayton's customers need boxes to ship produce abroad [k], which is why its order book has grown 25% in 9 months [app].

knowledge_max_2: Economic growth increases demand for goods and services
Rising exports increase demand for supporting domestic industries
application_max_2: Country X's economy grew by 3.8% last year, the fastest for a decade
Food exports have risen 14% and Drayton's order book has grown 25% in 9 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Drayton of recruiting 30 permanent workers.
questions.model_answer: Legal compliance and sustainable capacity: overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit [k], so relying on overtime risks breaching regulations while demand may rise another 20% [app], making recruitment of 30 workers necessary to keep output lawful and safe [an]. Contract security: permanent staff would let Drayton extend supply for two key customers over 3 years [k], securing stable order volumes [app], and this stability supports revenue planning and investment in the 2 factories [an].

knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff raises sustainable capacity
Overtime is limited by law and cannot expand indefinitely
application_max_2: Overtime is already at 12 hours per worker per week, close to the legal limit
Two key customers want their supply contracts extended for 3 years
analysis_max_2: Recruitment avoids breaking legal overtime limits while meeting demand
Permanent capacity secures long-term contracts and stable revenue

questions.question_text: Do you think Drayton should recruit 30 permanent workers? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Recruitment would let Drayton meet the projected 20% rise in orders next year [k], with 130 existing workers already on 12 hours overtime near legal limits [app], and would help secure two 3-year supply contracts, protecting a large share of $6.8 million revenue [an]. However, $900,000 a year in wages is a heavy permanent cost [k]; overtime and subcontracting cost an extra $250,000 a year and avoid long-term commitments if demand falls [app], so a downturn could leave 30 extra workers idle and profit fragile [an]. On balance, Drayton should recruit the 30 workers [eval], because the evidence of sustained growth (25% order growth, GDP at 3.8%) makes long-term capacity cheaper and safer than overtime [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Recruiting permanent staff meets rising demand with sustainable capacity
Recruitment adds permanent wage costs and risk if demand falls
application_max_2: Projected orders rise another 20% over the next 12 months with overtime near legal limits at 12 hours
Recruitment costs $900,000 a year versus $250,000 extra for overtime and subcontracting
analysis_max_2: Permanent staff secure capacity for 3-year contracts and revenue growth
If demand disappoints, 30 extra workers become an expensive burden
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on recruiting the 30 workers
Judgement weighs sustained growth evidence against permanent wage risk

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Ainsworth Active Leisure operates 2 leisure centres in Country X, with a gym, swimming pool and fitness classes at each. It employs 64 staff and has 3,800 members paying an average of $42 per month, generating revenue of $2.7 million last year. Inflation is at 8.5% and interest rates are at 7%; Country X's consumer confidence index has fallen from 105 to 88. Some 620 members have cancelled or downgraded in 6 months.

Centre manager Lucy Hammond must decide how to respond. Option 1 is to cut standard membership from $42 to $35, which would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join (3,800 x $7). Option 2 is to launch an off-peak membership at $25 for mornings only, aimed at retirees and job-seekers, without cutting standard prices. Renewals are due for 1,500 members next quarter.

questions.question_text: Define 'consumer confidence'.
questions.model_answer: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel about the economy and their own finances. Higher confidence encourages spending; low confidence makes consumers save instead of spend. [2]

knowledge_max_2: Consumer confidence is how optimistic consumers feel
High confidence encourages spending; low confidence encourages saving

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why gym membership at Ainsworth has fallen recently.
questions.model_answer: High inflation reduces real incomes: inflation of 8.5% means wages buy less, so consumers cut non-essential spending [k]; Ainsworth has lost 620 members in 6 months [app]. Low consumer confidence: the index has fallen from 105 to 88, so households feel pessimistic about their finances [k], and a $42 monthly leisure membership is an easy budget item to cancel [app].

knowledge_max_2: High inflation reduces consumers' purchasing power
Low consumer confidence reduces willingness to spend on non-essentials
application_max_2: Inflation is at 8.5% with interest rates at 7%
Some 620 members have cancelled or downgraded in 6 months

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Ainsworth of launching an off-peak membership at $25.
questions.model_answer: Fills quiet morning capacity: gyms are often under-used before noon [k], and an off-peak $25 membership could attract retirees and job-seekers looking for affordable exercise [app], turning empty capacity into extra revenue without cutting standard prices [an]. Protects standard fees: standard members keep paying $42, avoiding the $26,600 monthly loss a full cut would cause [k], while the off-peak tier widens the market to price-sensitive groups [app], building the membership base to offset the 620 cancellations [an].

knowledge_max_2: Off-peak pricing monetises spare capacity at quiet times
A separate tier avoids discounting existing customers
application_max_2: The off-peak membership at $25 targets mornings, retirees and job-seekers
A full cut would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join
analysis_max_2: Quiet morning capacity becomes revenue without diluting standard prices
A wider membership base offsets cancellations and protects total income

questions.question_text: Do you think Lucy Hammond should cut standard membership from $42 to $35? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A cut could win back some of the 620 cancelled or downgraded members [k], and at $35 Ainsworth might still keep more members paying something than losing $42 fees entirely [app], protecting footfall and class income across the 2 centres [an]. However, cutting the fee reduces income by $26,600 a month before any new members sign up [k], and an off-peak membership at $25 targets price-sensitive customers without discounting everyone [app], so a full cut may be unnecessarily deep while 1,500 renewals are due next quarter [an]. On balance, Ainsworth should launch the $25 off-peak membership rather than cut standard fees [eval], because the risk of losing $26,600 a month outweighs the uncertain gains from the cut [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Lowering price can stimulate demand and win back lapsed members
A price cut reduces revenue from existing members unless demand rises sharply
application_max_2: A cut from $42 to $35 would reduce fee income by $26,600 a month before any new members join
620 members have cancelled or downgraded; 1,500 renewals are due next quarter
analysis_max_2: Retaining price-sensitive customers protects footfall and ancillary income
The fixed monthly loss applies immediately while new sign-ups are uncertain
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the membership price cut
Judgement weighs certain monthly revenue loss against uncertain demand recovery

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Emmer & Oak Bakery is a family-run partnership in Country X, supplying fresh bread and rolls to 140 schools under a 12-month fixed-price contract worth $1.6 million. It employs 48 staff and delivered 2.1 million loaves last year. Since the contract was signed, inflation in Country X has reached 10%. Flour costs are up 35%, yeast and packaging up 18%, and oven energy bills up 25%.

Partner Mira Castellanos estimates the contract will lose the bakery $90,000 over its remaining 5 months if prices are not changed. She can either ask the schools' caterer to renegotiate the contract now, risking cancellation if the caterer switches to a rival bakery, or continue at the agreed price until the contract ends and then quote a higher price at renewal. The caterer has written a 3-month notice period into the contract.

questions.question_text: Outline what is meant by a 'fixed-price contract'.
questions.model_answer: A fixed-price contract is an agreement where the price stays the same for a set period, no matter how costs change. It gives the buyer price certainty but can hurt the supplier if costs rise. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A fixed-price contract keeps the price unchanged for a set period
Fixed-price contracts give the buyer certainty but shift cost risk onto the supplier

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Emmer & Oak's costs have increased.
questions.model_answer: Rising raw material costs: inflation of 10% has pushed flour prices up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18% [k], so every one of the 2.1 million loaves costs more to produce [app]. Higher energy bills: oven energy costs have risen 25% [k], which is significant for a bakery running ovens throughout the day [app].

knowledge_max_2: Inflation raises raw material costs
Inflation raises energy and utility costs
application_max_2: Flour costs are up 35% and yeast and packaging up 18%
Oven energy bills are up 25% for a bakery delivering 2.1 million loaves a year

questions.question_text: Explain two risks for Emmer & Oak of asking the caterer to renegotiate now.
questions.model_answer: Loss of the contract: if the caterer refuses and invokes the 3-month notice period, the bakery could lose a $1.6 million contract to a rival [k], cancelling roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and putting 48 jobs at risk [app], leaving the ovens idle and fixed costs uncovered [an]. Damaged relationships: challenging a signed contract may make the caterer distrust future deals [k], and the schools' caterer may warn other public buyers about the bakery [app], making it harder to win the renewal or new contracts [an].

knowledge_max_2: A buyer may cancel a contract under the notice period if asked to renegotiate
Challenging a contract can damage the supplier-buyer relationship
application_max_2: The caterer has written a 3-month notice period into the contract
The contract is worth $1.6 million a year supplying 140 schools, with 48 staff dependent on it
analysis_max_2: Cancellation removes roughly $133,000 of monthly revenue and threatens jobs
Reputation damage reduces the chance of winning the renewal or future bids

questions.question_text: Do you think Mira Castellanos should ask the caterer to renegotiate the contract now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Renegotiating now could stop the bakery losing $90,000 over its remaining 5 months [k], and with flour up 35% and oven energy up 25%, continuing at the agreed price is unsustainable for 48 staff [app], so an honest conversation backed by cost evidence might be accepted by the caterer [an]. However, renegotiation risks cancellation under the 3-month notice period, losing $1.6 million a year [k], and the caterer could simply switch to a rival bakery rather than pay more mid-contract [app], leaving the bakery with idle ovens and wages it cannot cover [an]. On balance, Mira should wait until renewal and quote a higher price then, while absorbing a controlled loss now [eval], because protecting a 12-month customer relationship is worth more than $90,000 [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Renegotiating can recover rising costs on a fixed-price contract
Renegotiating risks cancellation and losing the customer
application_max_2: The contract will lose $90,000 over its remaining 5 months at current costs
The caterer has a 3-month notice period and could switch to a rival bakery
analysis_max_2: Successful renegotiation stops the $90,000 loss and stabilises margins
Cancellation removes $1.6 million of annual revenue and threatens jobs and capacity
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on renegotiating now
Judgement weighs the certain $90,000 loss against the risk of losing the whole contract

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Bramcote Homes is a private limited company in Country X, building family houses on a 9-hectare site. It has completed Phases 1 and 2 — 60 houses — and employs 85 construction and office staff. Phase 2 sold out in 8 months at an average price of $240,000. The central bank has cut its base rate twice this year, from 6% to 4%, and mortgage approvals have risen 30%.

Director Farah Qureshi plans Phase 3 with 24 houses costing $4.8 million to build. The bank has offered a loan of $1.5 million at 5%, repayable over 10 years with interest of about $75,000 a year. Bramcote holds retained profit of $2.2 million. Farah must decide whether to start Phase 3 now, launching in the spring selling season, or wait 6 months until rates fall further and use more retained profit to shrink the loan. House prices rose 3% last year.

questions.question_text: Define 'mortgage'.
questions.model_answer: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property, repaid with interest over many years. For most households it is their largest single debt. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A mortgage is a long-term loan used to buy property
A mortgage is repaid with interest over many years

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why demand for Bramcote Homes' new houses may rise when interest rates fall.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper mortgage repayments: cutting the base rate from 6% to 4% lowers monthly mortgage payments on a $240,000 average house [k], putting home ownership within reach of more buyers [app]. Higher mortgage approvals: approvals across Country X have risen 30% since the cut [k], showing that more households are being approved to borrow [app].

knowledge_max_2: Lower interest rates reduce mortgage repayments
Lower interest rates make banks more willing to lend
application_max_2: Bramcote sells houses at an average price of $240,000 on a 9-hectare site
Mortgage approvals have risen 30% after the cut from 6% to 4%

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Bramcote of borrowing $1.5 million at 5% to start Phase 3 now.
questions.model_answer: Starting now matches buyer demand: mortgage approvals have risen 30% and rates are at 4% [k], so launching 24 houses in the spring selling season after Phase 2 sold out in 8 months captures buyers at peak confidence [app], potentially generating revenue near $5.76 million (24 x $240,000) [an]. Retained profit stays available: the loan of $1.5 million at 5% costs about $75,000 a year in interest [k], leaving Bramcote's $2.2 million retained profit as a cushion for overheads and delays [app], which protects cash flow if any houses sell slowly [an].

knowledge_max_2: Starting at a peak-demand moment maximises sales
Borrowing preserves internal finance for other needs
application_max_2: Phase 2 sold out in 8 months and mortgage approvals have risen 30%
The loan of $1.5 million at 5% costs about $75,000 a year, leaving $2.2 million retained profit intact
analysis_max_2: Early launch captures peak demand and raises revenue
Preserving retained profit protects cash flow against delays

questions.question_text: Do you think Farah Qureshi should borrow $1.5 million at 5% to start Phase 3 now? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: Starting now could secure strong sales: mortgage approvals are up 30% and Phase 2 sold out in 8 months, so 24 houses launched in spring could sell quickly [k], revenue potential near $5.76 million against $75,000 a year interest [app], lifting profit and strengthening Bramcote's market position [an]. However, borrowing now means $75,000 a year interest for 10 years, and rates might fall further, making a larger retained-profit contribution cheaper later [k]; waiting 6 months could let Farah shrink the loan and reduce interest [app], but house prices rose 3% last year and competitors may launch first, eroding first-mover advantage [an]. On balance, Farah should start Phase 3 now with the loan [eval], because demand evidence (approvals up 30%) outweighs the modest risk of slightly higher interest [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Starting now exploits peak demand and first-mover advantage
Borrowing creates fixed interest costs that are worse if rates fall later
application_max_2: Mortgage approvals have risen 30% since the cut from 6% to 4%
$1.5 million loan at 5% costs about $75,000 a year over 10 years
analysis_max_2: Early launch maximises revenue and market position
Waiting could reduce interest costs but risks losing buyers to rivals
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on borrowing to start Phase 3 now
Judgement weighs demand evidence against interest-rate uncertainty

unit: Unit 6: External Influences on Business Activity
scenario_stem:
Clearbrook Logistics is a private limited company operating a distribution depot in Country X, employing 140 drivers, warehouse workers and office staff. It delivers 1,900 tonnes of goods a week for supermarket customers and recorded revenue of $5.2 million last year. Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, and Clearbrook has 25 unfilled driver vacancies despite advertising for 4 months.

Operations director Mr Ellison must decide how to respond. One option is to raise driver wages by 10%, adding $3,400 a year for each of its 96 drivers, a total of $326,400 a year. The other option is to launch an in-house training scheme costing $60,000 to recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience. Two rival firms have already raised wages by 8%.

questions.question_text: Identify two problems a very low unemployment rate can cause a business.
questions.model_answer: One problem is a shortage of available workers, making it hard to fill vacancies. A second problem is pressure to raise wages to attract and keep staff, increasing costs. [2]

knowledge_max_2: A shortage of available labour makes recruitment harder
Low unemployment creates upward pressure on wages

questions.question_text: Explain two reasons why Clearbrook is struggling to recruit drivers.
questions.model_answer: Few unemployed workers: regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record, so almost all qualified drivers already have jobs [k], which is why Clearbrook has 25 unfilled vacancies after 4 months of advertising [app]. Rivals are competing for the same workers: two rival firms have already raised wages by 8% [k], so Clearbrook's current pay is no longer competitive [app].

knowledge_max_2: A shortage of labour makes filling vacancies difficult
Rival firms may outbid a business for scarce workers
application_max_2: Regional unemployment has fallen to 2.1%, the lowest on record
25 driver vacancies remain unfilled after 4 months of advertising

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits to Clearbrook of launching the in-house training scheme costing $60,000.
questions.model_answer: Cheaper than a 10% wage rise: the scheme costs $60,000 once, versus $326,400 a year extra for a wage rise across all 96 drivers [k], freeing cash for other needs such as vehicle maintenance [app], so profit is protected while vacancies are filled [an]. Grows a committed workforce: training 25 local people with no prior driving experience builds loyalty [k], and they arrive without holding rival offers created by the 8% wage rises elsewhere [app], reducing the risk of trained drivers simply leaving for competitors [an].

knowledge_max_2: In-house training can be cheaper than a general wage increase
Training internally can build loyalty and reduce turnover
application_max_2: The scheme costs $60,000 versus $326,400 a year for a 10% wage rise across 96 drivers
It would recruit and licence 25 local people with no prior driving experience
analysis_max_2: Lower one-off cost protects profit and cash flow
Loyal new drivers reduce the risk of poaching by rivals

questions.question_text: Do you think Mr Ellison should raise driver wages by 10%? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer: A 10% rise would match or beat rivals who have raised wages by 8% [k], adding $3,400 a year per driver and costing $326,400 a year across 96 drivers [app], which should stop current drivers leaving and make the 25 vacancies easier to fill [an]. However, $326,400 a year is a permanent increase to fixed costs [k], while the $60,000 training scheme creates 25 locally recruited drivers who may stay loyal for years [app], and it could deliver capacity faster than hoping the tight labour market frees up qualified drivers [an]. On balance, Clearbrook should launch the training scheme rather than raise all wages by 10% [eval], because $60,000 versus $326,400 a year is strongly better value for filling the vacancies [eval].

knowledge_max_2: Raising wages helps attract and retain scarce labour
Raising wages permanently increases fixed costs
application_max_2: A 10% rise adds $3,400 a year per driver and $326,400 a year across 96 drivers
The alternative training scheme costs $60,000 once to licence 25 local people
analysis_max_2: Competitive wages stem turnover and fill vacancies
A permanent wage increase erodes profit if demand or margins weaken
evaluation_max_2: Justified recommendation on the 10% wage rise
Judgement weighs $326,400 a year against a one-off $60,000 training cost
